Young Entrepreneur

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight on Carte Blanche: A teenager from Pretoria becomes the youngest commercial aquaponic farmers in the country and doing so with foresight and expertise.

Unique Selling Point:
Rikalize is a 16 year old teenager and owner of one of the largest aquaponic farms in South Africa. She does this without the help of her father. Instead the business is run from her cellphone during the week when she is at school and weekends she is hands on. She has a small team of reliable operating staff responsible for the day to day duties of growing fish and plants which she sells to restaurants and hotels in Pretoria.


Summary:
Rikalise is a teenager with a passion for aquaponics and a drive to succeed. She started off with a home-made tank and 1000 fish at the age of 12. Today she has 88 000 Tilapia in her tanks and runs one of the four biggest aquaponic farms in South Africa at the tender age of 16.

She has also invented a filtration system to clean ‘dirty’ water. This earned her a gold medal at the Eskom Science Expo for ‘own design on reuse of effluent water`. The system is called Decoupled Aquaponic System (DAPS) Through this technique she has cut her water consumption from 2 500 liters per day to 450 litres.

In her greenhouse she houses 22 plant species (vegetables, herbs and sweet melons) which she sells to restaurants. She sells about 400 plants each week. What is amazing about her is that she makes enough money from her farming the she pays all her overheads herself, pay two salaries, buy fish food and electricity and still pump some money back into the business to buy more fry (baby fish).

Her dad has taught her to build her own tanks, connect pipes and run the business by herself.
She is an example of a young entrepreneur who have achieved in 4 years what most teenagers will only dream of.


Further information:
“My name is Rikalize Reinecke, and I am 16 years old”. I am the owner of an Aquaponic farm in South Africa outside Pretoria. I started this farm in January 2012 when I was 12 year old.”
This is how Rikalize Reinecke introduces herself on her website.

Rikalize Reineke is a girl with a passion for aquaponics. She is the youngest fish farmer in the country with 88 000 Tilapia fish in her tanks and 22 plant species in her greenhouse tunnels that she grows hydroponically. She is the only person in South Africa that sells aquaponic products in her own shop and also supply on a bi-monthly basis fresh produce and fish to a number of restaurants in Pretoria.

More background:
Her inspiration and fascination with aquatic animals started four years ago when she watched “Dolphin Tale,” a story about a dolphin who gets caught in a trap in the ocean and damages her tail. Rescued by a marine biologist who designs a prosthetic for the dolphin the animal is able to swim again. Rikalize was hooked. She decided there and then that she wanted to study fish. But first where to start? Farming with fish seemed to be the obvious choice for a schoolgirl living on a farm where space was plenty and borehole water available.

She persuaded her father to send her on course in Grahamstown where she learnt the basics about commercial fish farming, or aquaculture. On return her father, an electrical engineer by trade, helped her to build a small fish dam where she started with 1000 Tilapia fish. “My ignorance and uncontrollable enthusiasm meant I kept on adding more fish without planning the filtration system properly. I soon realised that I wasted so much water every day to keep the fish dam clean that I had to come up with a solution”, she says. Aquaponics was the natural choice as this allowed her to use the waste, effluent water from the fish dam and use it to grow plants. Soon her fish farming business expanded to a true aquaponic farming method, a symbiotic relationship where aquatic animals and plant material are ‘grown’ simultaneously.

Her aquaponic farming grew from strength to strength and today she is probably the youngest female person in the country to farm commercially using hydroponics and aquaculture in symbiosis to utilise as little fresh water as possible and grow vegetables organically without any pesticide or fertilisers.

Over and above her enthusiasm and success as an aquaponic farmer she has designed a home kit perfect for NGOs that will enable them to have a yield of fresh produce and fish to eat using very little fresh water and with minimal startup cost. The kit costs R14 000 but thereafter supplies enough vegetables and fish for a small community. Her next goal is to include a solar system that allows this kit to run without Eskom energy supply thus enabling the buyer to be totally off the grid.

Our story will track ‘a day in the life of’ this young girl and how she functions with school work, and still get time to manage her business from a distance on her cellphone. Though remote control visual on her cell - captured on a series of cameras - she is able to the farming activities and give instructions to her right-hand, Carlos Kambanga, a Malawian who joined her in 2015 and shares her passion and skills for aquaponics.

Aquaponics is the way of the future as nutrient rich waste water from fish in in rearing tanks is used to provide plant food to vegetables and herbs grown hydroponically in grow-beds. Plants in the grow-beds grow rapidly in response to dissolved nutrients as well as the micro-climate within the greenhouse.

Aquaponics is a sustainable food production system combining conventional aquaculture in a symbiotic environment. This farming method is sustainable, environmentally friendly and at the same time water-wise. The fish farming in symbiosis with the plant farming is a perfect solution for the future in producing organic food free of pesticide and harmful chemicals in our food.

Press Release:


The Youngest Aquaponics Farmer
Combining aquaculture and hydroponic farming methods, aquaponics farming is breaking new ground in agriculture. It is a difficult and complex undertaking for even the most experienced farmers, but 16-year-old scholar, Rikalize Reinecke still manages to operate one of the largest aquaponics farms in the country. Carte Blanche meets this extraordinary entrepreneur.


Script:


FINAL Script: Young Entrepreneur
24 April 2018
Duration: 8 minutes

V/O Rikalize Reinecke is sixteen years old. She attends a school in Pretoria and on weekends goes home to a farm in the Roodeplaat dam area near Cullinan.

Up audio

V/O When Rikalize was just twelve years old she started researching how to become a fish farmer.

Claire Mawisa: how does a 12 year old decide they want to work with fish?

Rikalize Reinecke: Aquaponics farmer - Fish is my passion and since I was little I always had this interesting factor about fish. I did some research and came to the point that there is not going to be no fish left in the ocean for me to work on as marine biologist. So then I saw I could do something to prevent that and that is how I became a fish farmer.

V/O She asked her father for advice.

Claire Mawisa: At what point did you realise she is quite serious about this thing with fish?

Danie Reinecke: Rikalize’s Father: She was asking about this fish thing quite a few times then she wanted to do it in the Roodeplaat dam and then i said no you can’t do that. And then one day she came to me with a printout she got from the internet and she said “here! You can do it on land!

V/O Rikalize later attended a course in Grahamstown called Aquaculture Farming Management. This was a four day workshop on how to breed fish in a controlled environment. She was the youngest student.

Danie Reinecke: And on our way back she punched me she says ”now I am qualified.” And then it struck me ‘ok you made a promise.’

V/O Together they built the first two fish tanks, filled it with fresh water and
1000 fish. Rikalize chose Tilapia as they were easy to breed, fast growers and a popular fish served in restaurants. Eager to grow her business, she built two more dams and doubled the fish quantity in each tank.  
Rikalize Reinecke: So then my father said we have 4 dams let’s try to put 1000 fish in each dam and then the problem came, the ammonia was too high.

V/O Rikalize realized that by doubling up on the number of fish the waste increased and the water became toxic. She turned to aquaponics as a solution. In an aquaponic system, nutrient-rich wastewater from fish in the breeding tanks is used to provide plant food to vegetables and herbs grown hydroponically in grow-beds. The removal of nutrients from the water by the plants allows the newly cleaned water to be recirculated back into the fish tank.

Rikalize: Aquaponics is very intensive, small surface area, you are working with water and you recycle your water and instead of adding compost and fertiliser your fish is the fertiliser.

Claire Mawisa: So you told your father what you wanted to do, what role did he play in setting up the business?

Rikalize Reinecke: His arrangement was he was going to do it once, I can look, the second time he is going to help me, the third time he is going to look and I need to do it on my own.

V/O Her father taught her the practical skills but marketing her product was another challenge.

Rikalize Reinecke: I did not know a market is very important to supply your vegetables or fish to so i build up this system with a lot of vegetables and a lot of fish and i did not know who to sell it to.

V/O Then a few months later, she got her first order.

Rikalize Reinecke: Then a company approached me and said they wanted some fish,1 tone per month. And that is how it was just growing from opportunity.

V/O The aquaponic farming was now becoming to a profitable business. She found a shop near Pretoria where the public and her customers and suppliers could purchase
directly. She employed Maria Rudolph to run the shop.

Up audio

Rikalize Reinecke: About weekly we get a thousand new plants. All our plants go to different clients we try and focus everything mainly to our shop. But we have 22 different species of crops in our tunnels. I never thought it was going to grow into a business. My only idea was 1000 fish and 2 dams.

V/O With the demand for her fresh fish and plants growing every month, Rikalize thought of way to use less water in her farming process. By doubling up on the plants to clean the waste-water of the fish she could save up to 4000 litres of water every day. She called it the decoupled aquaponic system or DAP.

Rikalize Reinecke: So due to the fact that I just added plants and a lot of biosurface area where good bacteria can grow I can clean my water in an 8 hour cycle.

Link: It is here on the farm where Rikalize puts in the long hours to make a success of her business. Unlike other teenagers she has the responsibilities of any other business woman.

Up audio: The iron in the system is very low..

V/O She employes 3 full time staff. Carlos Kambangah is her right hand man overseeing the farm during the week while Rikalize is at school.

Claire Mawisa: How did it happen that you knew about fish?

Carlos Kambangah: Aquaponic farm assistant: Since I started working here in 2015 then the second month Rikalize sent me to the course, then I do the fish learning course.

Claire Mawisa: And what are your responsibilities?

Carlos Kambangah: My responsibility is to take care for everything that is here when Rikalize is not around.

Claire Mawisa: And she says when she is not here you are the man in charge, is that true?

Carlos Kambangah: Exactly that is true. 100%

Rikalize Reinecke: So this is the hatchery, slash nursery, in this system I breed all my own fish.

V/O On the farm there are now 88 thousand fish and 16 dams. And in the greenhouse tunnels there are 22 different species of plants growing producing 2.86 tons per year.

Claire Mawisa: She has done so much more than you ever thought she would. What growth have you seen in your child in that 4 years?

Danie Reinecke: She is so extremely responsible. As a parent you get a shock sometimes to think that that is the responsibility she has taken.

Link: Rikalize attends boarding school here in Pretoria but every weekend goes home to look after her business. Every single morning she uses her phone to check up on what’s happening on her aquaponics farm outside Cullinan.

Rikalize Reinecke: I have a very good high tech camera system all around the facility. Usually once a day I will log into the system zoom into the different cameras and from there I can send a message to the workers telling them to please do this or go and look for that.

Audio up: Danie explaining to Rikalize on the power failure.

V/O Rikalize’s father is also a specialist in surveillance systems set up the cameras for her to help identify problems early on.

Rikalize Reinecke: So if there is a power failure I will get a message saying “alpha system power failure”. I will usually give them 5 minutes to just to start the generator to see what’s wrong. If the power is not on with in 5 minutes I will call them so even though I am still at class I will make a plan.

V/O Rikalize is constantly thinking of new ideas. She designed a mini version of her aquaponic system in a modular kit form.

Rikalize Reinecke: I have release a smaller system, and my vision for that system is to put it all around africa. A person can grow his own vegetables and he has fish. I believe there is a big gap in the market for this industry to grow and I believe this is the future of farming.

V/O Rikalize has proved that nothing is impossible, even for a young teenager. In 2016 she won the Gold medal at the Eskom Science Expo for her DAP system: was a guest speaker in 2107 at the World Aquaculture convention and workshopped in the Virgin Islands with a world leader in the field of the Aquaponics, Dr. James Rakocy; and 2018 back home, she was chosen to exhibit her modular system at the Gauteng Innovative Technology conference.

Uudio up; family around the table

V/O Rikalize has a strong family support, in many small ways they lend a hand to ease the burden of a business that has grown beyond expectation.

Claire Mawisa: What do you foresee in the future? Your child is a force of nature, your child.

Danie Reinecke: If she keeps doing the hard work that she is doing now and staying humble I think she will achieve what she wants to achieve.

Up audio:

Rikalize: I learnt to make very hard decisions. I have been in a situation where I have to choose between, friends, and fun and business.

Claire Mawisa: Do you ever sit back and think wow?

Rikalize Reinecke: When I do that then I just get more ideas. So my father said I should rather not think about that.

She found a shop near Pretoria where the public and her customers and suppliers could purchase directly. She employed Maria Rudolph to run the shop. Up audio Rikalize Reinecke: About weekly we get a thousand new plants. All our plants go to different clients we try and focus everything mainly to our shop. But we have 22 different species of crops in our tunnels. I never thought it was going to grow into a business. My only idea was 1000 fish and 2 dams. V/O With the demand for her fresh fish and plants growing every month, Rikalize thought of way to use less water in her farming process. By doubling up on the plants to clean the waste-water of the fish she could save up to 4000 litres of water every day. She called it the decoupled aquaponic system or DAP. Rikalize Reinecke: So due to the fact that I just added plants and a lot of biosurface area where good bacteria can grow I can clean my water in an 8 hour cycle. Link: It is here on the farm where Rikalize puts in the long hours to make a success of her business. Unlike other teenagers she has the responsibilities of any other business woman. Up audio: The iron in the system is very low.. V/O She employes 3 full time staff. Carlos Kambangah is her right hand man overseeing the farm during the week while Rikalize is at school. Claire Mawisa: How did it happen that you knew about fish? Carlos Kambangah: Aquaponic farm assistant: Since I started working here in 2015 then the second month Rikalize sent me to the course, then I do the fish learning course. Claire Mawisa: And what are your responsibilities? Carlos Kambangah: My responsibility is to take care for everything that is here when Rikalize is not around. Claire Mawisa: And she says when she is not here you are the man in charge, is that true? Carlos Kambangah: Exactly that is true. 100% Rikalize Reinecke: So this is the hatchery, slash nursery, in this system I breed all my own fish. V/O On the farm there are now 88 thousand fish and 16 dams. And in the greenhouse tunnels there are 22 different species of plants growing producing 2.86 tons per year. Claire Mawisa: She has done so much more than you ever thought she would. What growth have you seen in your child in that 4 years? Danie Reinecke: She is so extremely responsible. As a parent you get a shock sometimes to think that that is the responsibility she has taken. Link: Rikalize attends boarding school here in Pretoria but every weekend goes home to look after her business. Every single morning she uses her phone to check up on what’s happening on her aquaponics farm outside Cullinan. Rikalize Reinecke: I have a very good high tech camera system all around the facility. Usually once a day I will log into the system zoom into the different cameras and from there I can send a message to the workers telling them to please do this or go and look for that. Audio up: Danie explaining to Rikalize on the power failure. V/O Rikalize’s father is also a specialist in surveillance systems set up the cameras for her to help identify problems early on. Rikalize Reinecke: So if there is a power failure I will get a message saying “alpha system power failure”. I will usually give them 5 minutes to just to start the generator to see what’s wrong. If the power is not on with in 5 minutes I will call them so even though I am still at class I will make a plan. V/O Rikalize is constantly thinking of new ideas. She designed a mini version of her aquaponic system in a modular kit form. Rikalize Reinecke: I have release a smaller system, and my vision for that system is to put it all around africa. A person can grow his own vegetables and he has fish. I believe there is a big gap in the market for this industry to grow and I believe this is the future of farming. V/O Rikalize has proved that nothing is impossible, even for a young teenager. In 2016 she won the Gold medal at the Eskom Science Expo for her DAP system: was a guest speaker in 2107 at the World Aquaculture convention and workshopped in the Virgin Islands with a world leader in the field of the Aquaponics, Dr. James Rakocy; and 2018 back home, she was chosen to exhibit her modular system at the Gauteng Innovative Technology conference. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tonight on Carte Blanche: A teenager from Pretoria becomes the youngest commercial aquaponic farmers in the country and doing so with foresight and expertise.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Rikalize is a 16 year old teenager and owner of one of the largest aquaponic farms in South Africa. She does this without the help of her father. Instead the business is run from her cellphone during the week when she is at school and weekends she is hands on. She has a small team of reliable operating staff responsible for the day to day duties of growing fish and plants which she sells to restaurants and hotels in Pretoria.
metadata.Summary: Rikalise is a teenager with a passion for aquaponics and a drive to succeed. She started off with a home-made tank and 1000 fish at the age of 12. Today she has 88 000 Tilapia in her tanks and runs one of the four biggest aquaponic farms in South Africa at the tender age of 16. She has also invented a filtration system to clean ‘dirty’ water. This earned her a gold medal at the Eskom Science Expo for ‘own design on reuse of effluent water`. The system is called Decoupled Aquaponic System (DAPS) Through this technique she has cut her water consumption from 2 500 liters per day to 450 litres. In her greenhouse she houses 22 plant species (vegetables, herbs and sweet melons) which she sells to restaurants. She sells about 400 plants each week. What is amazing about her is that she makes enough money from her farming the she pays all her overheads herself, pay two salaries, buy fish food and electricity and still pump some money back into the business to buy more fry (baby fish). Her dad has taught her to build her own tanks, connect pipes and run the business by herself. She is an example of a young entrepreneur who have achieved in 4 years what most teenagers will only dream of.
metadata.Further information: “My name is Rikalize Reinecke, and I am 16 years old”. I am the owner of an Aquaponic farm in South Africa outside Pretoria. I started this farm in January 2012 when I was 12 year old.” This is how Rikalize Reinecke introduces herself on her website. Rikalize Reineke is a girl with a passion for aquaponics. She is the youngest fish farmer in the country with 88 000 Tilapia fish in her tanks and 22 plant species in her greenhouse tunnels that she grows hydroponically. She is the only person in South Africa that sells aquaponic products in her own shop and also supply on a bi-monthly basis fresh produce and fish to a number of restaurants in Pretoria. More background: Her inspiration and fascination with aquatic animals started four years ago when she watched “Dolphin Tale,” a story about a dolphin who gets caught in a trap in the ocean and damages her tail. Rescued by a marine biologist who designs a prosthetic for the dolphin the animal is able to swim again. Rikalize was hooked. She decided there and then that she wanted to study fish. But first where to start? Farming with fish seemed to be the obvious choice for a schoolgirl living on a farm where space was plenty and borehole water available. She persuaded her father to send her on course in Grahamstown where she learnt the basics about commercial fish farming, or aquaculture. On return her father, an electrical engineer by trade, helped her to build a small fish dam where she started with 1000 Tilapia fish. “My ignorance and uncontrollable enthusiasm meant I kept on adding more fish without planning the filtration system properly. I soon realised that I wasted so much water every day to keep the fish dam clean that I had to come up with a solution”, she says. Aquaponics was the natural choice as this allowed her to use the waste, effluent water from the fish dam and use it to grow plants. Soon her fish farming business expanded to a true aquaponic farming method, a symbiotic relationship where aquatic animals and plant material are ‘grown’ simultaneously. Her aquaponic farming grew from strength to strength and today she is probably the youngest female person in the country to farm commercially using hydroponics and aquaculture in symbiosis to utilise as little fresh water as possible and grow vegetables organically without any pesticide or fertilisers. Over and above her enthusiasm and success as an aquaponic farmer she has designed a home kit perfect for NGOs that will enable them to have a yield of fresh produce and fish to eat using very little fresh water and with minimal startup cost. The kit costs R14 000 but thereafter supplies enough vegetables and fish for a small community. Her next goal is to include a solar system that allows this kit to run without Eskom energy supply thus enabling the buyer to be totally off the grid. Our story will track ‘a day in the life of’ this young girl and how she functions with school work, and still get time to manage her business from a distance on her cellphone. Though remote control visual on her cell - captured on a series of cameras - she is able to the farming activities and give instructions to her right-hand, Carlos Kambanga, a Malawian who joined her in 2015 and shares her passion and skills for aquaponics. Aquaponics is the way of the future as nutrient rich waste water from fish in in rearing tanks is used to provide plant food to vegetables and herbs grown hydroponically in grow-beds. Plants in the grow-beds grow rapidly in response to dissolved nutrients as well as the micro-climate within the greenhouse. Aquaponics is a sustainable food production system combining conventional aquaculture in a symbiotic environment. This farming method is sustainable, environmentally friendly and at the same time water-wise. The fish farming in symbiosis with the plant farming is a perfect solution for the future in producing organic food free of pesticide and harmful chemicals in our food. Our story
